title: The Landscaper's Guide to Modern Sales & Marketing
author: Jack Jostes
description: Weekly video and podcast series helping lawn and landscape contractors attract quality customers to increase profits and improve lifestyle, hosted by Amazon best-selling author Jack Jostes.

episodes.title: How Transparency, Pricing & AI Are Changing Landscape Sales
episodes.summary: Chuck Harkins of Miller Landscape talks about selling to customers who research pricing and competitors before they ever call. The conversation covers transparent pricing, video marketing, sales metrics, and where AI fits into a modern landscape sales process.

episodes.title: Choosing Better Work: How Frank Di Sandro Built a More Profitable Landscape Business
episodes.summary: Frank Di Sandro of Di Sandro Landscape Group explains how being selective about jobs and applying the 80/20 rule moved his company from low-margin maintenance into higher-margin construction and hardscaping. He also covers video marketing and accountability with marketing partners.

episodes.title: How Berns Landscaping Cut 20-Hour Snow Events in Half
episodes.summary: Logan Berns and Matt Cunningham explain how bigger crews, more reliable equipment, pretreatment, and better technology cut their exhausting snow events roughly in half. They stress that tech should support crews, not replace their judgment.

episodes.title: From Barber Shop to Fractional CMO: Faith, AI, and Betting Big with Drew Dinkelacker
episodes.summary: Drew Dinkelacker shares his path from barber shop owner to fractional CMO and how AI becomes a real process-improvement tool once workflows are documented. The conversation also covers decision-making frameworks and timing a big expansion.

episodes.title: 40 Years Residential-Only. Now He's Going Commercial.
episodes.summary: Scott Benson explains how Benson Landscape is adding commercial snow services after four decades of residential-only work. Topics include targeted outreach, developing leaders, and marketing more than one service line at once.

episodes.title: From Operator to Owner: The 5 Identity Shifts Every Landscape Business Owner Must Make
episodes.summary: Author Jason Swenk joins Jack Jostes to walk through the five identity shifts a founder makes on the way from solo operator to true owner. They cover documenting systems, delegating outcomes instead of tasks, spotting natural leaders, and the self-sabotage that shows up at each stage.

articles.question: How do I stop working in my business and start working on it?
articles.metaDescription: Jason Swenk and Jack Jostes lay out the five identity shifts from operator to owner, plus how to document systems, delegate outcomes, and spot leaders.
articles.intro: You stop working in your business by changing who you are inside it, one stage at a time, not by hiring a manager and hoping. On The Landscaper's Guide to Modern Sales & Marketing, host Jack Jostes talks with author Jason Swenk about the five identity shifts a founder goes through: operator, manager, architect, CEO, and owner. The practical moves are documenting what you do before you hand it off, delegating outcomes instead of tasks, and expecting the guilt that shows up when you finally step back.

sections.heading: The five stages between doing everything and owning everything
sections.body:
Swenk's framework starts where most landscape and home service owners live: the operator. You're the one estimating, selling, scheduling, and probably running a crew too. The next stage, manager, is where a lot of people get stuck. You've hired help, but now you're spending more hours checking their work than you ever spent doing it yourself.

The third stage is what Swenk calls the architect. Here your job is designing the systems that let other people make decisions without you. After that comes CEO, where you set direction, coach your leadership team, build relationships, and watch the numbers. The final stage is owner, which he describes as chairman of the board territory: you're accessible, but you're not needed day to day.

The point of naming the stages is that each one asks for a different version of you. The skills that made you a great operator actively hold you back as an architect.

quote.text: You're designing systems so other people can make decisions, you're not doing the work anymore.
quote.speaker: Jason Swenk

sections.heading: Record your screen before you write a single SOP
sections.body:
The advice that gets you unstuck from the manager stage is surprisingly low-tech. Swenk tells owners to record their screen while they do a task, narrating it as if they were training someone. That video then goes into an AI tool to produce a written procedure. You get a usable SOP without sitting down to write one from scratch, which is the step most owners never get around to.

He also suggests clearing out the cheap stuff first. Before you hand off anything important, get the ten-dollar tasks off your plate: the data entry, the invoice chasing, the scheduling shuffles. Those are easy to document, easy to hire for, and they free up the hours you'll need to build the bigger systems.

Do this in order. Document, then delegate. Hiring someone into a role that has no written process just creates a second operator who needs you for every decision.

quote.text: You're working probably 20 more hours a week managing people, doing their job.
quote.speaker: Jason Swenk

sections.heading: Hand people an outcome, not a checklist
sections.body:
One of the clearest ideas in the episode is the difference between delegating a task and delegating an outcome. If you give someone a list of steps, they'll come back to you the moment something falls outside the list. If you give them the result you want, they own the problem.

Swenk's example is marketing. Instead of assigning someone to post on social media three times a week, you tell them the outcome: more leads. They figure out the how. That's also how you find out who on your team can think like an owner and who needs more structure.

He's candid that hiring is a numbers game. Not every hire works out, and that's normal. The goal is to keep the process moving rather than treating each miss as proof that nobody can do it as well as you.

quote.text: You have to kiss a lot of toads to find your prince or princess.
quote.speaker: Jason Swenk

sections.heading: Spotting the leader who's already on your crew
sections.body:
When you're ready to move from architect to CEO, you need someone to run the day-to-day. Swenk offers a simple test: when you're gone, where does everyone go? If the crew consistently walks over to the same designer or foreman with questions, that person is already leading. Promote what's happening instead of recruiting a stranger to sit above them.

He also talks about matching your management style to the individual. Some people want autonomy, some want check-ins. Treating everyone the same is an operator habit, not a CEO one.

At the owner stage, Swenk still works, just far less. He describes himself as accessible for ten to twenty hours a week. That's the destination: available when it counts, absent from the routine.

quote.text: When you're gone, where do people go?
quote.speaker: Jason Swenk

sections.heading: The guilt is part of the process
sections.body:
The part of this conversation that most business advice skips is the emotional side. Swenk says owners routinely self-sabotage when they step out of a role. You feel guilty that you're not swinging a shovel or answering every call, and you drift back into work you already delegated.

His answer is to get clear on the new value you provide at each stage. As an architect, your value is the system. As a CEO, it's direction and coaching. If you can name what you're contributing, the guilt loses its grip. He even mentions that a period of low mood after a big shift is common, which is worth knowing before it happens to you.

quote.text: A lot of times you'll self sabotage and you'll feel guilty.
quote.speaker: Jason Swenk

keyTakeaways: Founders move through five identities: operator, manager, architect, CEO, and owner. Each needs a different skill set.
Document tasks by recording your screen and narrating, then use AI to turn the video into a written procedure.
Delegate outcomes like "get more leads" rather than step-by-step task lists, so people own the problem.
Find your next leader by noticing who the team already goes to when you're not around.
Expect guilt and self-sabotage when you step back, and counter it by naming the new value you provide.

faq.q: What should I delegate first in a small landscaping business?
faq.a: Start with the low-value, repetitive tasks Swenk calls ten-dollar tasks, such as data entry, scheduling, and invoice follow-up. They're easy to document and hire for, and they free up hours for building real systems.

faq.q: How do I write SOPs without spending weeks on them?
faq.a: Record your screen while doing the task and talk through it as if you're training someone. Feed the recording into an AI tool to generate the written procedure, then clean it up.

faq.q: How many hours does an owner work once they've stepped back?
faq.a: Swenk says he stays accessible and works roughly ten to twenty hours a week at the owner stage. The exact number depends on the business, but the goal is being available for big decisions, not daily operations.

articles.sourceNote: Based on the August 7, 2026 episode of The Landscaper's Guide to Modern Sales & Marketing, "From Operator to Owner: The 5 Identity Shifts Every Landscape Business Owner Must Make," hosted by Jack Jostes with guest Jason Swenk.
